screens.title: Command Pattern: Encapsulating Requests
screens.narratorSegment: We begin by seeing the Command pattern as a way to wrap a request — an instruction — into its own object. That object contains everything needed to perform the action: the operation, any parameters, and a reference to the receiver that actually executes it. This makes commands portable: you can store them, queue them, log them, or reverse them later. A concrete example is a home automation remote. Instead of the remote calling device methods directly, each button holds a command object. Pressing a button simply calls Execute on that object, and the command takes care of the device-specific work. Why this matters: decoupling reduces ripple changes when you add devices, and it makes undo and macro sequences possible. Over the next screens we will examine the ICommand interface, receivers like Light and GarageDoor, concrete commands, an invoker implementation, how undo stacks work, and how to avoid common mistakes like overusing commands for trivial operations. Notice how this pattern appears in editors, transaction systems, and task queues — anywhere you want control over how requests are recorded and replayed. As you go through the lesson, think about a real feature you might build: what would be the receiver, what data must a command carry, and how would you undo it?

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practice & Safety
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives screen focuses on hands-on skills and safety checks. You will build a small remote-control style invoker that sets and invokes command objects, then extend it with an undo mechanism using a history stack. screens.title: What the Command Pattern Is
screens.narratorSegment: The Command pattern packages a request as an object that exposes at least an Execute operation and often an Undo. This command object contains any parameters and, crucially, a reference to the receiver that will perform the real work. The benefit is twofold: callers become blind to implementation details, and command objects become first-class units that can be queued, logged, stored, or reversed. For a concrete example, imagine the remote control sending a 'TurnOn' request. Instead of directly calling a Light's TurnOn method, the remote calls Execute on a command object that knows which Light to control. A common misconception is thinking this pattern is only for GUI buttons. In truth, it's useful wherever you need to treat actions as data — for scheduling, auditing, or batch execution. A pitfall is overuse: wrapping trivial calls that will never be queued or undone adds boilerplate and object churn. To check your understanding, ask: could I represent this action as an object with its own state and still keep each command focused on a single responsibility? What the Command Pattern Is means command objects make operations portable and decouple who asks from who does the work.. In practical terms, define a request object and what it enables. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › What the Command Pattern Is
Command = Request as Object
A command carries the operation, parameters, and a receiver reference so it can be executed later or undone.
Elements
  • ICommand: Execute, Undo.
  • ConcreteCommand: Binds a receiver and an action.
  • Invoker: Triggers commands without knowing receivers.
  • Receiver: Implements action logic.
Key Takeaway
Treat actions as objects when you need flexibility, history, or queuing.
Analogy: A Post-It Instruction
A command is like a Post-It with a clear instruction and the address of who should carry it out. You can hand it to someone, file it, or stick it on a to-do list to run later.
Concrete Example
Remote button calls Execute on a LightOnCommand; the command calls the Light receiver's TurnOn method.
Common Mistake
Wrapping trivial, never-queued operations in commands adds unnecessary complexity and memory overhead.

screens.title: Invoker, Command, Receiver Roles
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the roles clarifies why the pattern decouples code. The Invoker issues requests by calling a command's Execute method; it does not know which receiver will handle the task. The Command object holds a reference to a Receiver and translates the Execute call into concrete receiver method calls. The Receiver contains the domain logic — for example, a Light knows how to turn on and off, and a GarageDoor knows how to open and close. The layered separation allows multiple commands to reference the same receiver, and an invoker to operate on any command that implements the ICommand contract. A concrete remote-control architecture uses seven slots: each slot stores an on and off command. An undo reference holds the last executed command for reversal. A frequent misconception is to conflate invoker and receiver; remember the invoker triggers and the receiver acts. Also, adding a new device does not require changing the invoker — you only create new concrete commands. With this mental model you can design an invoker that stores command history, a queue for asynchronous processing, or macro commands that compose multiple concrete commands.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Invoker, Command, Receiver
Layered Architecture
Keep invoker, commands, and receivers separate so responsibilities stay focused and changes are localized.
Invoker (RemoteControl)
Stores commands, calls Execute, and can keep an undo reference.
Command (LightOnCommand)
Holds receiver reference and implements Execute and Undo.
Receiver (Light)
Performs the concrete actions.
Example: Remote Slots
A RemoteControl may hold arrays of onCommands and offCommands and a field to reference the last executed command for undo. No change to RemoteControl is needed when adding new device types.
Design Notes
  • Keep each command focused on one operation to respect single responsibility.
  • Use NoCommand to avoid null checks for empty slots.
Check Your Understanding
Identify which class is responsible for state changes and which only references state-changing methods.

screens.title: ICommand: Interface and Responsibilities
screens.narratorSegment: At the heart of the pattern is the ICommand contract. In our C# examples it declares Execute and often Undo. Execute performs the operation; Undo reverses it. Design decisions for the interface matter: do you need Undo for every command? If not, Undo can be a no-op or omitted, but having it supports a unified undo stack. Also consider exceptions: Execute should handle failures or bubble them in a way the invoker can manage, and Undo should carefully restore state or report inability to undo. A concrete example: LightOnCommand's Execute calls the Light receiver's TurnOn, while Undo calls TurnOff. For DeleteText in a text editor, DeleteTextCommand must capture the deleted substring during Execute so Undo can re-insert it later. A common misconception is that Undo simply reverses Execute; in reality, Undo must account for side effects and state that may have changed since Execute. When designing ICommand, document expected semantics for Execute and Undo and ensure each concrete command contains sufficient state to perform undo safely. Consider adding asynchronous execution support if commands may be heavy. In practical terms, what execute and undo must provide and why. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Execute performs the action; Undo reverses it and may require stored state. Implementations must handle exceptions and side effects carefully.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › ICommand Interface
ICommand Contract
Expect Execute() for action and Undo() to reverse it. Implementations must store any data needed to undo.
C# Snippet
public interface ICommand
{
  void Execute();
  void Undo(); // Optional but recommended for undo/redo
}
Misconception
Undo is not always a simple inverse of Execute; it often needs captured state to restore faithfully.
Example: DeleteTextCommand
When deleting, the command should store the deleted substring during Execute so Undo can re-add it. Without storing that state, Undo cannot restore the original content.
Design Tip
If commands may be long-running, consider adding ExecuteAsync or running Execute inside a Task so the UI thread remains responsive.

screens.title: Concrete Commands and Receivers
screens.narratorSegment: Concrete commands implement the ICommand interface and encapsulate a receiver reference and any parameters needed to perform the action. For example, LightOnCommand stores a Light receiver and calls its TurnOn method in Execute, and TurnOff in Undo. GarageDoorOpenCommand keeps a GarageDoor receiver and calls Open, with Undo calling Close. This binding is the glue that connects abstract intent to concrete behavior. A common mistake is letting concrete commands do too much work, violating single responsibility; instead they should delegate domain logic to the receiver and only translate the request. Another important point is reuse: multiple commands can reference the same receiver instance. For example, LightOnCommand and LightOffCommand both reference a LivingRoom Light. When implementing commands, capture only the state necessary for undo and avoid duplicating domain logic inside commands. A short design check: when a command needs to restore state on undo, ensure it stores the minimal snapshot required — like a deleted substring or prior visibility flag — rather than copying entire complex objects unnecessarily. In practical terms, how commands bind to receivers and call methods. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Concrete Commands
LightOnCommand (example)
public class LightOnCommand : ICommand
{
  private Light _light;
  public LightOnCommand(Light light) { _light = light; }
  public void Execute() { _light.TurnOn(); }
  public void Undo() { _light.TurnOff(); }
}
Note how the command delegates the real operation to the Light receiver without implementing the domain logic itself.
Guidelines
  • Store small snapshots for Undo, not full object copies when possible.
  • Keep commands focused: one responsibility per command.
  • Share receivers between commands rather than duplicating state.
Check
Can this command call only receiver methods and store minimal undo state? If yes, the design is clean.

screens.title: RemoteControl Invoker Walkthrough
screens.narratorSegment: The RemoteControl invoker pattern stores command objects in slots and triggers their execution without knowing receiver details. In the canonical C# version, the invoker keeps two arrays: one for onCommands and one for offCommands, and a field that holds the last executed command for undo. When a slot is set, SetCommand assigns the concrete commands for that slot. When OnButtonWasPushed or OffButtonWasPushed is called, the invoker calls Execute on the appropriate ICommand and records it as the undo candidate. UndoButtonWasPushed then calls Undo on the stored command. The NoCommand null object is crucial to avoid null checks in each slot — unassigned slots point to NoCommand which performs no action. A practical example: calling OnButtonWasPushed(0) triggers LightOnCommand. Execute which calls the Light receiver to turn on. If the user then pushes Undo, the invoker calls Undo on LightOnCommand which turns the light off. Remember to handle exceptions from Execute to avoid leaving the undo reference in an inconsistent state. This invoker design supports extension: add macro commands, queues, or async invocation paths without changing existing slots. In practical terms, how the invoker sets and triggers commands and supports undo. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Invoker behavior
keyIdea.text: Invoker stores commands, executes them via ICommand, and tracks the last command for undo. NoCommand avoids null checks.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › RemoteControl Invoker
RemoteControl Essentials
// Set an on/off command for a slot
remote.SetCommand(0, livingRoomLightOn, livingRoomLightOff);
// Execute
remote.OnButtonWasPushed(0);
// Undo last
remote.UndoButtonWasPushed();
Using a NoCommand default avoids nulls and keeps invocation simple: every slot always responds to Execute and Undo.
Invoker Safety
  • Wrap Execute calls in try/catch to maintain consistent undo state.
  • Decide how failed Execute affects the undo history — do not push failed commands.
  • Consider thread-safety if commands may be executed from multiple threads.
Example Outcome
Sequence: TurnOn, OpenGarage, TurnOff; Undo will reverse the most recent command first.

screens.title: Undo and Command History
screens.narratorSegment: Undo and redo depend on maintaining a history of executed commands. A simple approach is to push each successfully executed command onto a stack. Undo pops the top command and calls its Undo method. For redo, maintain a separate stack: when you undo a command, push it onto the redo stack; executing a new command clears the redo stack. Concrete example: in a text editor, executing AddTextCommand pushes that command to the undo stack; DeleteTextCommand stores the deleted substring and is also pushed. If the user chooses Undo, the editor pops the last command and calls Undo, which restores the previous text. A common misconception is treating undo as stateless reversal; undo must have access to the state snapshot captured when the command executed. Consider side effects like external resources or network calls: undoing them may require compensating actions, and sometimes true reversal is impossible. In those cases, document the limits and consider soft-undo mechanisms like creating an inverse compensating command or versioned state to restore. Design your history data structures to be memory conscious for long sessions and consider pruning or checkpointing older entries.

If the user chooses Undo, the editor pops the last command and calls Undo, which restores the previous text. In those cases, document the limits and consider soft-undo mechanisms like creating an inverse compensating command or versioned state to restore. Design your history data structures to be memory conscious for long sessions and consider pruning or checkpointing older entries.

keyIdea.title: Undo pattern
keyIdea.text: Push executed commands to an undo stack; pop and call Undo for reversal. Use a separate redo stack when needed and capture state required for reversal.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Undo & History
Undo / Redo Stacks
Push command on execute. Undo pops and calls Undo. For redo, pop from redo stack back onto undo.
Example: Text Editor
AddTextCommand stores the added text. On delete, DeleteTextCommand stores deleted substring. Undo uses stored data to restore content.
Limitations
  • Commands with external side effects may not be fully undoable.
  • Large histories cost memory; consider checkpointing or pruning.
  • Long-running operations may need compensating commands rather than strict undo.
Check
Can you capture the minimal state at execution time to reliably undo this action later?

screens.title: NoCommand Null Object and MacroCommand
screens.narratorSegment: Two practical extensions of Command are the NoCommand null object and MacroCommand composition. NoCommand is a concrete ICommand that does nothing on Execute and Undo. Using NoCommand as a default for unassigned invoker slots eliminates null checks and simplifies invoker logic. MacroCommand is a concrete command that holds a list of other commands and executes or undoes them in sequence. MacroCommand is useful when you want a single action to represent a series of steps — for example, a 'Good Night' macro that turns off lights, closes the garage door, and locks doors. screens.title: Performance Considerations and Mitigation
screens.narratorSegment: Commands are small objects and, in typical UI scenarios, the overhead is negligible compared to architectural benefits. However, a common performance pitfall occurs when a command's Execute performs heavy computation or input and output synchronously on the UI thread. For example, applying a large image filter inside Execute will pause the interface. To mitigate this, consider these strategies: run heavy commands asynchronously by providing ExecuteAsync or by wrapping Execute inside a Task, report progress back to the UI when long operations are required, and batch many tiny commands into a single MacroCommand to reduce object churn. Another approach is to use a dedicated thread pool or a background queue for heavy commands and keep the invoker responsive by scheduling rather than executing them inline. Also be mindful of memory when maintaining long undo histories — you can store compressed diffs, checkpoints, or prune older entries. The design decision depends on requirements: if strict synchronous semantics are not required, prefer async execution and progress reporting. Always profile the application to find real bottlenecks before optimizing prematurely. Executing heavy operations synchronously inside Execute blocks the UI and degrades user experience.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Design Guidance
screens.narratorSegment: The Command pattern can be misapplied. Common mistakes include creating commands for trivial operations that are never queued, logged, or undone; allowing concrete commands to contain complex domain logic rather than delegating to receivers; and forgetting to handle exceptions inside Execute which can corrupt history. To design correctly, adhere to single responsibility: each command should encapsulate one well-defined request. Use NoCommand to avoid null checks, and ensure Undo stores minimal, necessary state captured at Execute time. When commands interact with external systems or resources, document limited undoability and consider compensating commands for partial reversal. For performance, avoid many tiny command objects in tight loops — combine related operations into macro commands or batch updates at the receiver level. Finally, write tests that execute, undo, and redo sequences to validate correctness and resilience. A practical question to ask while designing: will this action ever need to be queued, logged, or reversed? If not, a direct method call might be simpler and clearer. In practical terms, avoid overuse and keep commands focused. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. screens.title: Where to Use the Command Pattern
screens.narratorSegment: The Command pattern shows up in many places. GUI applications use it for undo/redo in text editors and drawing programs; transaction systems encapsulate database operations as commands for commit or rollback; task schedulers queue commands for later or background execution; web APIs can represent requests as commands that validate, process, and log actions. A concrete example from the chapter is the remote control and its slots for lights and garage doors. fullNarratorScript:
We begin by seeing the Command pattern as a way to wrap a request — an instruction — into its own object. That object contains everything needed to perform the action: the operation, any parameters, and a reference to the receiver that actually executes it. This makes commands portable: you can store them, queue them, log them, or reverse them later. A concrete example is a home automation remote. Instead of the remote calling device methods directly, each button holds a command object. Pressing a button simply calls Execute on that object, and the command takes care of the device-specific work. Why this matters: decoupling reduces ripple changes when you add devices, and it makes undo and macro sequences possible. Over the next screens we will examine the ICommand interface, receivers like Light and GarageDoor, concrete commands, an invoker implementation, how undo stacks work, and how to avoid common mistakes like overusing commands for trivial operations. Notice how this pattern appears in editors, transaction systems, and task queues — anywhere you want control over how requests are recorded and replayed. As you go through the lesson, think about a real feature you might build: what would be the receiver, what data must a command carry, and how would you undo it?

By the end of these screens you will be able to explain and apply the Command pattern. First, you will define the core idea: a request is encapsulated as an object so callers can be parameterized and requests can be queued or logged. You will also identify practical scenarios where this pattern is helpful, such as building undo and redo, scheduling tasks for asynchronous execution, or logging actions for audit purposes. A concrete example is a remote control where each button holds a command object that calls a Light or GarageDoor receiver. Knowing when to use the pattern matters: use it when you need decoupling, undo, or queuing; avoid it for trivial one-off calls that add unnecessary object creation overhead. Finally, you will be able to implement the pattern in C#: define an ICommand interface, create concrete command classes that reference receivers, and write an invoker that stores, executes, and can undo commands. Each objective pairs a skill with a milestone you can verify by writing small C# examples and tests.

This second objectives screen focuses on hands-on skills and safety checks. You will build a small remote-control style invoker that sets and invokes command objects, then extend it with an undo mechanism using a history stack. A concrete practice is converting the starter TextEditor into a Command-based app with AddText and DeleteText commands and a stack to UndoLastAction. You will also learn safety patterns: use a NoCommand null object to avoid null checks on unassigned slots, and make commands handle receiver exceptions so the application remains stable. Finally, you will exercise design judgment: decide when to group small operations into macro commands to reduce overhead, and when to run heavy commands asynchronously. Each practice maps to a simple test you can run: set commands, execute them, call undo, and observe the document state. These exercises surface common mistakes and let you verify both correctness and responsiveness.

The Command pattern packages a request as an object that exposes at least an Execute operation and often an Undo. This command object contains any parameters and, crucially, a reference to the receiver that will perform the real work. The benefit is twofold: callers become blind to implementation details, and command objects become first-class units that can be queued, logged, stored, or reversed. For a concrete example, imagine the remote control sending a 'TurnOn' request. Instead of directly calling a Light's TurnOn method, the remote calls Execute on a command object that knows which Light to control. A common misconception is thinking this pattern is only for GUI buttons. In truth, it's useful wherever you need to treat actions as data — for scheduling, auditing, or batch execution. A pitfall is overuse: wrapping trivial calls that will never be queued or undone adds boilerplate and object churn. To check your understanding, ask: could I represent this action as an object with its own state and still keep each command focused on a single responsibility? What the Command Pattern Is means command objects make operations portable and decouple who asks from who does the work.. In practical terms, define a request object and what it enables. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Understanding the roles clarifies why the pattern decouples code. The Invoker issues requests by calling a command's Execute method; it does not know which receiver will handle the task. The Command object holds a reference to a Receiver and translates the Execute call into concrete receiver method calls. The Receiver contains the domain logic — for example, a Light knows how to turn on and off, and a GarageDoor knows how to open and close. The layered separation allows multiple commands to reference the same receiver, and an invoker to operate on any command that implements the ICommand contract. A concrete remote-control architecture uses seven slots: each slot stores an on and off command. An undo reference holds the last executed command for reversal. A frequent misconception is to conflate invoker and receiver; remember the invoker triggers and the receiver acts. Also, adding a new device does not require changing the invoker — you only create new concrete commands. With this mental model you can design an invoker that stores command history, a queue for asynchronous processing, or macro commands that compose multiple concrete commands.

At the heart of the pattern is the ICommand contract. In our C# examples it declares Execute and often Undo. Execute performs the operation; Undo reverses it. Design decisions for the interface matter: do you need Undo for every command? If not, Undo can be a no-op or omitted, but having it supports a unified undo stack. Also consider exceptions: Execute should handle failures or bubble them in a way the invoker can manage, and Undo should carefully restore state or report inability to undo. A concrete example: LightOnCommand's Execute calls the Light receiver's TurnOn, while Undo calls TurnOff. For DeleteText in a text editor, DeleteTextCommand must capture the deleted substring during Execute so Undo can re-insert it later. A common misconception is that Undo simply reverses Execute; in reality, Undo must account for side effects and state that may have changed since Execute. When designing ICommand, document expected semantics for Execute and Undo and ensure each concrete command contains sufficient state to perform undo safely. Consider adding asynchronous execution support if commands may be heavy. ICommand: Interface and Responsibilities means execute performs the action; undo reverses it and may require stored state. implementations must handle exceptions and side effects carefully.. In practical terms, what execute and undo must provide and why. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Concrete commands implement the ICommand interface and encapsulate a receiver reference and any parameters needed to perform the action. For example, LightOnCommand stores a Light receiver and calls its TurnOn method in Execute, and TurnOff in Undo. GarageDoorOpenCommand keeps a GarageDoor receiver and calls Open, with Undo calling Close. This binding is the glue that connects abstract intent to concrete behavior. A common mistake is letting concrete commands do too much work, violating single responsibility; instead they should delegate domain logic to the receiver and only translate the request. Another important point is reuse: multiple commands can reference the same receiver instance. For example, LightOnCommand and LightOffCommand both reference a LivingRoom Light. When implementing commands, capture only the state necessary for undo and avoid duplicating domain logic inside commands. A short design check: when a command needs to restore state on undo, ensure it stores the minimal snapshot required — like a deleted substring or prior visibility flag — rather than copying entire complex objects unnecessarily. Concrete Commands and Receivers means concrete commands link a receiver and an action, delegating domain logic to the receiver and storing only what is required to undo.. In practical terms, how commands bind to receivers and call methods. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The RemoteControl invoker pattern stores command objects in slots and triggers their execution without knowing receiver details. In the canonical C# version, the invoker keeps two arrays: one for onCommands and one for offCommands, and a field that holds the last executed command for undo. When a slot is set, SetCommand assigns the concrete commands for that slot. When OnButtonWasPushed or OffButtonWasPushed is called, the invoker calls Execute on the appropriate ICommand and records it as the undo candidate. UndoButtonWasPushed then calls Undo on the stored command. The NoCommand null object is crucial to avoid null checks in each slot — unassigned slots point to NoCommand which performs no action. A practical example: calling OnButtonWasPushed(0) triggers LightOnCommand. Execute which calls the Light receiver to turn on. If the user then pushes Undo, the invoker calls Undo on LightOnCommand which turns the light off. Remember to handle exceptions from Execute to avoid leaving the undo reference in an inconsistent state. Undo and redo depend on maintaining a history of executed commands. A simple approach is to push each successfully executed command onto a stack. Undo pops the top command and calls its Undo method. For redo, maintain a separate stack: when you undo a command, push it onto the redo stack; executing a new command clears the redo stack. Concrete example: in a text editor, executing AddTextCommand pushes that command to the undo stack; DeleteTextCommand stores the deleted substring and is also pushed. If the user chooses Undo, the editor pops the last command and calls Undo, which restores the previous text. A common misconception is treating undo as stateless reversal; undo must have access to the state snapshot captured when the command executed. Consider side effects like external resources or network calls: undoing them may require compensating actions, and sometimes true reversal is impossible. In those cases, document the limits and consider soft-undo mechanisms like creating an inverse compensating command or versioned state to restore. Design your history data structures to be memory conscious for long sessions and consider pruning or checkpointing older entries.

Two practical extensions of Command are the NoCommand null object and MacroCommand composition. NoCommand is a concrete ICommand that does nothing on Execute and Undo. Using NoCommand as a default for unassigned invoker slots eliminates null checks and simplifies invoker logic. MacroCommand is a concrete command that holds a list of other commands and executes or undoes them in sequence. MacroCommand is useful when you want a single action to represent a series of steps — for example, a 'Good Night' macro that turns off lights, closes the garage door, and locks doors. A misconception is thinking MacroCommand duplicates logic; instead it composes existing commands so each subcommand retains responsibility and undo semantics. When building macros, ensure you implement Undo by reversing the order of subcommands so each step is undone cleanly. Also consider error handling: if a subcommand fails during a macro, decide whether to roll back already executed subcommands or leave partial execution and report an error. These patterns increase robustness and reduce conditional complexity in the invoker. Commands are small objects and, in typical UI scenarios, the overhead is negligible compared to architectural benefits. However, a common performance pitfall occurs when a command's Execute performs heavy computation or input and output synchronously on the UI thread. For example, applying a large image filter inside Execute will pause the interface. To mitigate this, consider these strategies: run heavy commands asynchronously by providing ExecuteAsync or by wrapping Execute inside a Task, report progress back to the UI when long operations are required, and batch many tiny commands into a single MacroCommand to reduce object churn. Another approach is to use a dedicated thread pool or a background queue for heavy commands and keep the invoker responsive by scheduling rather than executing them inline. Also be mindful of memory when maintaining long undo histories — you can store compressed diffs, checkpoints, or prune older entries. The design decision depends on requirements: if strict synchronous semantics are not required, prefer async execution and progress reporting. Always profile the application to find real bottlenecks before optimizing prematurely. The Command pattern can be misapplied. Common mistakes include creating commands for trivial operations that are never queued, logged, or undone; allowing concrete commands to contain complex domain logic rather than delegating to receivers; and forgetting to handle exceptions inside Execute which can corrupt history. To design correctly, adhere to single responsibility: each command should encapsulate one well-defined request. Use NoCommand to avoid null checks, and ensure Undo stores minimal, necessary state captured at Execute time. When commands interact with external systems or resources, document limited undoability and consider compensating commands for partial reversal. For performance, avoid many tiny command objects in tight loops — combine related operations into macro commands or batch updates at the receiver level. Finally, write tests that execute, undo, and redo sequences to validate correctness and resilience. A practical question to ask while designing: will this action ever need to be queued, logged, or reversed? If not, a direct method call might be simpler and clearer. The Command pattern shows up in many places. GUI applications use it for undo/redo in text editors and drawing programs; transaction systems encapsulate database operations as commands for commit or rollback; task schedulers queue commands for later or background execution; web APIs can represent requests as commands that validate, process, and log actions.
